opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it comes down to a pretty simple observation: we're building some of the most powerful technology in human history, and we fundamentally don't understand how it works. We know how to train these models. We know the architecture, the loss function, the data. But what actually happens inside, the algorithms the network learns and the concepts it represents, is still largely a black box.

That matters for a few reasons. The first is reliability. If you're going to deploy a model in a high-stakes setting, like healthcare, finance, or critical infrastructure, you want more than "it did well on our evals." You want to know *why* it's making the decisions it's making, so you can tell when it's right for the right reasons and when it's right by accident or about to fail in a way you didn't anticipate.

The second is control. Right now the main ways we steer models are prompting and fine-tuning, which are pretty blunt instruments. You change some inputs or nudge some weights and hope the behavior moves in the direction you want. If you actually understand the internal representations, you can be much more surgical. You can find the feature responsible for a behavior and adjust it directly, or detect when a model is drifting into a mode you don't want.

The third, and maybe the biggest, is safety as these systems get more capable. As models get smarter, our ability to evaluate them from the outside gets weaker. If a model is smarter than you at some task, it's hard to check its work just by looking at outputs. Interpretability gives you a way to look under the hood and check whether the model's internal reasoning matches what it's telling you.

So I see interpretability as a bit like the transition from alchemy to chemistry. You can get a lot done by trial and error, but at some point, if you want to build things reliably and safely, you need a real science of what's going on inside. I think that's where AI is right now, and it's why I'm so excited to be working on it.

r001.rationale: The response argues that interpretability helps make AI more reliable, controllable, and safe, but does not claim that intentionally designing AI as a new generation of software requires techniques for exposing neural networks’ inner workings.

r002.rationale: The response compares AI development to alchemy before chemistry, not to steam engines preceding thermodynamics.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that we're building systems whose capabilities are growing much faster than our understanding of them, and I don't think that gap is sustainable.

Today, when you train a large model, you're essentially growing it rather than designing it. You set up an objective, you pour in data and compute, and out comes something that can write code, reason through math problems, carry on conversations. But nobody wrote the program that does those things. It emerged. And when we open it up, what we see is billions of numbers, not an explanation.

That matters for a few reasons. The first is just trust. We're going to deploy these systems in medicine, in law, in infrastructure, in places where a wrong answer has real consequences. Right now, when a model makes a decision, the best we can do is ask it to explain itself, and the explanation it gives may or may not reflect what actually happened inside. That's not a standard we'd accept for a bridge or an airplane.

The second is safety in a deeper sense. If a model has learned something we didn't intend, a shortcut, a hidden goal, a tendency to behave differently when it thinks it's being watched, we want to be able to see that directly rather than hoping it shows up in a benchmark. Behavioral testing only catches what you think to test for. Looking inside gives you a chance at catching what you didn't anticipate.

And the third is more optimistic. These models have learned real structure about the world. They have internal representations of concepts, of relationships, of how things work. If we can read those representations, interpretability stops being just a safety tool and becomes a way to actually learn from the models, to understand what they've discovered, and to build better ones on purpose instead of by accident.

So I'd frame it this way: interpretability is how we move from being alchemists to being engineers. And I think the next phase of AI really depends on making that transition.

r001.rationale: The candidate says interpretability could help build better models on purpose, but does not clearly claim that intentionally designing a new generation of software requires techniques that expose neural networks’ internal workings.

r002.rationale: The candidate makes no analogy to steam engines preceding thermodynamics or to technological progress preceding understanding of underlying principles.

astra-6.text:
I think the central issue is that our ability to build powerful neural networks has outpaced our ability to understand them. We can train a system, measure its performance, and see that it does remarkable things, but that doesn’t necessarily tell us how it arrived at an answer or when it’s going to fail.

As we give these systems more responsibility, that gap matters more. You want to understand whether a model has learned something robust or whether it’s relying on a shortcut that happens to work in your tests. And when something goes wrong, you want to be able to diagnose it and make a targeted fix.

Understanding the internals won’t solve every safety problem. But it could give us a much stronger foundation for deciding when to trust these systems—and for building better ones.

r001.rationale: The response says understanding neural network internals could help diagnose failures and build better systems, but it does not claim that intentionally designing AI as a new generation of software requires techniques that expose those internals.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention steam engines, thermodynamics, or an equivalent analogy about technological progress preceding understanding.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the core issue is that our ability to build powerful neural networks has outpaced our ability to understand them. We can measure how well a model performs, but that doesn’t necessarily tell us how it arrived at an answer or when its behavior might break down.

As we give these systems more responsibility, that gap matters. We want to understand whether a model has learned something robust or found a shortcut that works on our tests. Understanding the internal mechanisms could help us diagnose failures, improve reliability, and make more informed decisions about where to deploy these systems.

That doesn’t mean we need to understand every neuron before a model can be useful. But if AI is going to become a technology we increasingly depend on, we need better ways to explain and predict its behavior than simply observing that it usually works.
